title: The Organic Food Myth: Science Versus Marketing
summary: An explainer separating organic food's lower synthetic pesticide residue from its lack of a meaningful nutrient advantage, and flagging healthy-user bias.

assertions.quote: organic fruits and vegetables do not hold significantly more vitamins
Organic farming successfully leaves measurably less synthetic pesticide residue on the final product
No single study proves that eating organic food alone acts as a shield against disease.
Those impressive health metrics are likely the result of this entire package of habits.

verdicts.note: Regular organic consumers tend to be more educated, higher-income, active, health-conscious and plant-leaning, and the authors say benefits seen in observational studies may partly reflect diet quality and lifestyle.

High organic consumers were more often female, higher-income, better educated, more active, leaner, and ate more fibre, fruit and vegetables and less meat, and the authors list residual confounding as a limitation.

Regular organic eaters exercised more, smoked less and ate less red and processed meat, but socioeconomic differences were small (33% vs 31% in the upper third), so the healthier part holds more clearly than the wealthier part.
ERS reports organic consumers have always been fairly diverse in income, race and ethnicity, though price remains a barrier for some; it does not address health or confounding.

The authors argue that organic consumption is a complex behaviour that adjustment cannot fully capture, and that NutriNet-Sante's organic-cancer associations were confined to subgroups likelier to buy organic, raising residual confounding; this is their argument, not a measurement.

assertions.quote: Eating a high volume of fruits and vegetables is vastly more important for your body than whether or not those items have an organic sticker
regular conventional produce in the United States is perfectly safe
